title: Unit final: graphs
sub: New problems to recognize, an islands trace, a Union-Find trap and explaining out loud
cards/0/q: New problems. Match the statement to the technique.
cards/0/pairs/0/0: Walls and Gates (#286): distance from every room to the nearest gate
cards/0/pairs/0/1: BFS from all gates at once
cards/0/pairs/1/0: Course Schedule II (#210): return the order of courses
cards/0/pairs/1/1: The order of leaving Kahn's queue
cards/0/pairs/2/0: Max Area of Island (#695): the area of the largest island
cards/0/pairs/2/1: The traversal returns the cell count
cards/0/pairs/3/0: Accounts Merge (#721): accounts sharing an email belong to one person
cards/0/pairs/4/0: Open the Lock (#752): 4 wheels of 10 digits, forbidden combinations
cards/0/pairs/5/0: Surrounded Regions (#130): fill regions that don't touch the border
cards/1/q: Shortest Bridge (LeetCode #934): an n×n grid up to 100×100 with exactly two islands. What is the minimum number of water cells to fill in to connect them? How do you solve it in O(n²)?
cards/1/options/0: Mark the first island with a traversal and put all its cells in the queue; BFS through water level by level up to the first cell of the second island
cards/1/options/1: A separate BFS from each cell of the first island to the second, then take the minimum
cards/1/options/2: DFS from the first island through water: the first path that reaches the second is the shortest
cards/1/options/3: Union-Find: merge water cells with islands until the islands are in one group
cards/1/explain: This is lesson 1 plus lesson 2: a traversal finds the first island, and all of it becomes one source of a multi-source BFS. The wave moves through water, and the level at which it touches the second island is the number of filled cells plus one. Each cell enters the queue once — O(n²).
cards/1/wrong/1: The answer is right, but an island has up to n² cells and each BFS is up to n²: O(n⁴) in total, up to 10⁸ at 100×100. That's exactly the repeated work a single BFS from all sources removes.
cards/1/wrong/2: The path along which DFS reached the target need not be the shortest: DFS follows one line as far as it goes. Fewest steps means BFS only.
cards/1/wrong/3: Union-Find answers “are they connected”, not “how many cells to fill”: it knows nothing about distances.
cards/2/q: Number of Operations to Make Network Connected (LeetCode #1319): up to 10⁵ computers and a list of cables. Any cable can be moved to another pair of computers. How many moves are needed to connect them all, or −1?
cards/2/options/0: If there are fewer than n − 1 cables — −1; otherwise the number of components minus 1, which Union-Find gives
cards/2/options/1: The number of cables on which Union returned false: each redundant one has to be moved
cards/2/options/2: n − 1 minus the number of cables: that's how many a tree is missing
cards/2/options/3: The number of components: each one needs to be attached with one cable
cards/2/explain: Connecting n vertices takes at least n − 1 edges — with fewer cables it can't be done. If there are enough, spare cables can always be found: k components are joined by k − 1 moves, one for each component except the first. Union-Find counts the components in one pass over the cables, Count at the end.
cards/2/wrong/1: There can be more redundant cables than moves needed: one component may have several, while the number of moves is exactly the number of components to attach.
cards/2/wrong/2: The number of cables doesn't tell you how many components there are. On 4 computers with a triangle 0–1–2 there are 3 = n − 1 cables, the formula gives 0, but computer 3 isn't connected: 1 move is needed.
cards/2/wrong/3: The first component is already in place: the others need attaching, k − 1.
cards/3/task: A new 5×5 map with lots of corner contacts. Step through the island count; the rig will ask twice what happens next.
cards/3/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: The calls return, and the loop finds (0, 3) — island #2
cards/3/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Sink sinks (2, 2): it touches (1, 1) at a corner
cards/3/goal/asks/0/q: (1, 1) is sunk. Below, right and left are water, above is the already sunk (0, 1). Diagonally, at (2, 2), there's land. What next?
cards/3/goal/asks/0/explain: Neighbors share a side only, so (2, 2) isn't part of island #1. Sink unwinds, control returns to the outer loop, and the loop goes row by row: row 0 comes before row 2, so the first untouched land is (0, 3).
cards/3/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: (4, 4) is already part of island #4: it's diagonal from (3, 3)
cards/3/goal/asks/1/q: (4, 2) is sunk, island #5 is done. What next?
cards/3/goal/asks/1/explain: The side neighbors of (4, 4) are (3, 4) and (4, 3), both water; it touches (3, 3) only at a corner. So island #4's DFS never reached it, it's still '1', and the loop finds it as island #6. With eight neighbors this whole map would be a single island.
cards/4/q: Counting components of an undirected graph (#323). On n = 3 with edges [[0,1],[1,2],[0,2]] the code returns 0, but the answer is 1. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/4/explain: The counter drops on every edge, not on every merge. The third edge [0,2] joins vertices already in one group: a == b, there's no merge, but count-- runs anyway. It needs if (a == b) continue; before merging — that's the false of Union from lesson 5. On a tree the bug is invisible: every edge there merges.
cards/5/q: Open the Lock (#752): a lock of 4 wheels with digits 0–9, a move turns one wheel by ±1, the start is "0000", some combinations are forbidden. Fewest moves to the target. How much work does BFS do?
cards/5/options/0: 10⁴ states with 8 moves from each — up to 8·10⁴ transitions: BFS is instant
cards/5/options/1: 10⁸: compare every combination with every other
cards/5/options/2: 4! = 24 states: the wheels can only be rearranged
cards/5/options/3: Infinite: the wheels turn in circles, so BFS loops forever
cards/5/explain: Count the state space before coding: 4 wheels of 10 positions — 10⁴ strings, and from each, 4 wheels × 2 directions = 8 neighbors. Forbidden combinations go into visited up front, so they're never entered. Loops are harmless: visited keeps any state from being entered twice.
cards/5/wrong/1: Nobody compares pairs: neighbors are generated — 8 per state, like the 26 letters in Word Ladder.
cards/5/wrong/2: The wheels aren't rearranged but turned: a state is four digits, not their order.
cards/5/wrong/3: There are finitely many states, and visited marks each one when it's pushed: every state enters the queue at most once.
cards/6/q: Unity, an RTS: a 512×512 map, 300 player units must retreat from the nearest of 200 enemies, and the enemies move. What do you compute?
cards/6/options/0: One distance map, a BFS from all enemies at once every few frames; a unit steps to the neighbor with a larger distance
cards/6/options/1: A BFS from every unit to the nearest enemy every frame
cards/6/options/2: A* from every unit to the cell farthest from the enemies
cards/6/options/3: Union-Find over cells: a unit moves into another component
cards/6/explain: “Distance to the nearest of many” is a multi-source BFS: 2.6·10⁵ cells in one pass serve every unit at once. The enemies move, so the map is rebuilt — but every few frames, not once per unit.
cards/6/wrong/1: The answer is the same, but it's 300 traversals instead of one, each up to the whole map in the worst case: up to 300 · 2.6·10⁵ ≈ 8·10⁷ cells per frame.
cards/6/wrong/2: The farthest cell still has to be found — with the same distance map — and then come 300 path searches. The distance map itself already says where to step.
cards/6/wrong/3: Connected components don't depend on where the enemies are: units and enemies are almost always in the same component. You need distances, and Union-Find doesn't provide them.
cards/7/q: You are solving Shortest Bridge out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/7/items/0: Clarify: side neighbors, exactly two islands, the answer is the number of cells filled
cards/7/items/1: Naive: a BFS from every cell of the first island — O(n⁴)
cards/7/items/2: Idea: find the first island with a traversal and make all its cells the sources of a single BFS
cards/7/items/3: Code: a traversal with marking, then a level-order BFS through water to a cell of the second island
cards/7/items/4: Run it on a small grid where one water cell separates the islands
cards/7/items/6: Edge cases: islands touching at a corner, a one-cell island
cards/7/explain: First agree on connectivity and on what counts as the answer — the “minus one” at the end depends on it. Then the naive baseline, an idea built from two known parts, the code, a run-through, the cost and the edges: touching at a corner is not a connection.
cards/8/q: Complexity of the unit's solutions. What is true? Select all.
cards/8/options/0: Number of Islands is O(m·n) time
cards/8/options/2: Union-Find with union by rank and path compression is almost O(1) per operation, amortized
cards/8/options/3: A multi-source BFS from k sources is O(k·m·n)
cards/8/options/4: #1293 is O(m·n): each cell enters the queue once
cards/8/options/5: Recursive DFS on a 300×300 grid of solid land is safe with a 1 MB stack
cards/8/explain: Islands: each cell once; Kahn: each vertex and each edge once; Union-Find: O(α(n)), α ≤ 4. A multi-source BFS is one traversal: all sources in one queue, O(m·n) for any k. In #1293 the queue holds states, not cells: O(m·n·k). Recursion over 9·10⁴ cells of solid land takes 5–9 MB of stack.
